paragraphs.text: Familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (FAME) is an autosomal dominant disorder defined by a core triad of cortical tremor, multifocal myoclonus, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures (Crompton et al., 2012). Corbett et al. (2019) noted that symptoms of cortical myoclonic tremor usually start in the second decade of life, and that overt myoclonic or generalized tonic-clonic seizures follow. Expressivity varies within and between families. Guerrini et al. (2001) described the chromosome 2-linked disorder in an Italian pedigree as autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME), with complex partial seizures in some patients.

paragraphs.text: Guerrini et al. (2001) studied a pedigree with 8 affected individuals. The disorder was nonprogressive and began between ages 12 and 50 years. All patients had predominantly distal, semicontinuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 had complex partial seizures. Most affected individuals had seizures only rarely and had normal cognition. However, the 3 individuals with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. All patients had frontotemporal as well as generalized interictal EEG abnormalities. Neurophysiologic study pointed to a cortical origin of the myoclonus. In 5 patients there was EEG-EMG coherence at 8 to 25 Hz over the contralateral rolandic area, with EEG activity preceding EMG activity by 8 to 15 ms. The C-reflex at rest was enhanced, and somatosensory and visual evoked potentials were of high amplitude. On transcranial magnetic stimulation, the resting motor threshold was significantly reduced and the postmotor evoked potential silent period was significantly shortened. The authors suggested that these findings reflected diffuse cortical hyperexcitability. They named the disorder autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME).

paragraphs.text: Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy. Eleven members, aged 24 to 56 years (mean 39.2 years), had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 of them had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study confirmed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members. Three presymptomatic members had giant somatosensory evoked potential components and an enhanced long-loop reflex I. All 3 developed hand tremor and upper limb myoclonus after 1.5 years of follow-up.

Neurophysiologic findings suggested increased excitability of the primary motor cortex, with normal sensorimotor integration.

paragraphs.text: Crompton et al. (2012) studied a 6-generation FAME kindred of European descent, ascertained in New Zealand and Australia. All 55 affected members had fine hand tremor, which typically began in adolescence (median age 15 years; range 4 to 60 years). Forty-four of the 55 (80%) had proximal myoclonus, which began later than the hand tremor (median age 17 years; range 5 to 60 years). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of the 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range 18 to 76 years). These seizures occurred around sleep onset following severe generalized myoclonus. Neurophysiologic testing confirmed features of cortical reflex myoclonus. The most common phenotype in this family was mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, combined with subtle proximal myoclonus.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) described a second ADCME family from Tuscany (family B). This 4-generation kindred had 5 affected members, 4 of them living. All patients had postural myoclonus of the hands and upper limbs, and cortical tremor was the presenting symptom in every case, beginning between ages 18 and 50 years. All but 1 patient had epilepsy, mainly rare generalized tonic-clonic seizures, sometimes triggered by visual stimuli. Two patients also had drug-resistant focal motor or complex partial seizures. One patient had borderline cognitive level, and the others had normal intelligence. All patients had generalized or focal paroxysmal EEG activity. Jerk-locked back-averaged EEG, somatosensory evoked potentials, and long-loop reflexes were consistent with cortical reflex myoclonus. None of the ADCME patients had cardiovascular disease. Two of the oldest mutation carriers developed age-related dementia. The authors also noted that myoclonus often worsened at older ages.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) summarized the clinical features of 22 FAME2 families. Most were Italian, and the others were of Australian/New Zealand, Iraqi and Israeli Sephardic Jewish, South African, French, French/Spanish, and Syrian origin. The frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures ranged from 15 to 100% across families. Seizures were usually controlled with antiepileptic drugs for generalized epilepsies, although a few individuals had drug-resistant epilepsy. In the large Australian/New Zealand family, Corbett et al. (2019) found evidence of anticipation. Median age at onset of any relevant symptom was 30 years in generation III (n = 6), 17 years in generation IV (n = 30), and 12 years in generation V (n = 16).

paragraphs.text: Guerrini et al. (2001) performed genome-wide linkage analysis in their ADCME family. They identified a 12.4-cM critical region on chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2, between markers D2S2161 and D2S1897. The maximum 2-point lod score was 3.46 at theta = 0.0 for marker D2S2175, and multipoint lod scores reached 3.74 around D2S2175. Linkage to the familial adult myoclonic epilepsy locus on chromosome 8q23.3-q24 was excluded.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) sequenced candidate genes in the critical region in the original Tuscan ADCME family (family A) that had been reported by Guerrini et al. (2001). They identified a novel in-frame insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B gene, c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG, which replaces 5 amino acids (HGGAL) with 4 residues (QFGR) in the third intracellular loop (p.H225_L229delinsQFGR). The indel cosegregated completely with the disease. It was absent from 575 unrelated controls from Tuscany and from public databases, a total of 16,080 chromosomes. The same indel was found in a second Tuscan ADCME family (family B), which shared the disease haplotype across the entire critical region. Targeted capture and next-generation sequencing of the coding regions in the critical region in 2 affected members of family A identified no other relevant change. The authors did not detect ADRA2B mutations in southern Italian BAFME pedigrees linked to the same locus. In functional studies, the mutant receptor localized normally to the plasma membrane and was internalized in an arrestin-3-dependent manner. However, it could not form a stable complex with spinophilin after epinephrine stimulation. In Xenopus oocytes, spinophilin did not raise the EC50 for epinephrine with the mutant receptor as it did with wildtype. The authors concluded that the mutation increased the intensity of epinephrine-stimulated calcium signaling, a gain-of-function effect.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from 2 individuals in the Australian/New Zealand family, 1 from an Italian family, and 3 from a French-Spanish family. They found expansion of an ATTTT repeat and insertion of an ATTTC repeat within the first intron of the STARD7 gene in all FAME samples tested. The ATTTC repeat was absent from whole-genome sequencing data of 69 controls. Using repeat-primed PCR, they detected the expansion in 137 of 137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported FAME2 families. Two of 24 relatives without a FAME diagnosis also carried the expansion, and both were from younger generations and likely presymptomatic. Of 72 additional individuals with features similar to FAME, all 20 familial cases from 6 families and 1 of 52 singleton cases carried the expansion. In total, the ATTTC expansion segregated in 158 of 158 typically affected individuals from 22 pedigrees. It was also present in 8 of 13 family members whose FAME diagnosis was uncertain. The ATTTC repeat primer was 100% sensitive for FAME in all families with linkage or suggestive linkage to chromosome 2. These included 2 families with the ADRA2B variant reported by De Fusco et al. (2014), and Corbett et al. (2019) concluded that this variant was likely not causative. Long-read sequencing showed the repeat structure. One individual from the Australian/New Zealand family had a SMRT read with 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats and a nanopore read with 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats, which suggested somatic variation in repeat size. An individual from another family had 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats. In patient-derived fibroblasts, STARD7 transcript and protein levels were unaltered, and RNA-seq showed no reads containing ATTTC repeats.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) identified an in-frame indel in the ADRA2B gene, c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG, which replaces 5 residues (HGGAL) with 4 (QFGR) in the third intracellular loop (p.H225_L229delinsQ225_F_G_R228). They found it in affected members of 2 Tuscan families with autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy. The indel cosegregated completely with the disease and was absent from 575 Tuscan controls and from public databases. The mutant receptor failed to form a stable complex with spinophilin after agonist activation and increased epinephrine-stimulated calcium signaling. Corbett et al. (2019) later found that the 2 families carrying this variant also carried the STARD7 intronic ATTTC repeat expansion, which strongly suggested that the ADRA2B allele is not causative.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of 22 FAME2 families of diverse origin, Corbett et al. (2019) identified an inserted, expanded ATTTC pentanucleotide repeat, together with an expanded endogenous ATTTT repeat, in the first intron of the STARD7 gene. On the forward strand of chromosome 2, the repeat had the structure (AAATG)n(AAAAT)n. The expansion was found by whole-genome sequencing and repeat-primed PCR. It segregated in 158 of 158 typically affected individuals and was absent from 69 control genomes and 28 control DNA samples. Long-read sequencing of one patient showed 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats in a SMRT read and 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats in a nanopore read, which suggested somatic instability. Another patient had 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats, 4,645 bp in total. STARD7 mRNA and protein levels were not altered in patient fibroblasts.

checks.claim: Corbett et al. (2019) studied affected members of 22 FAME2 families of diverse origin.
checks.evidence_quote: The ATTTC expansions segregate in 158/158 individuals typically affected by FAME from 22 pedigrees including 16 previously reported families recruited worldwide.

checks.claim: In affected members of FAME2 families, an inserted, expanded ATTTC pentanucleotide repeat was identified in the first intron of the STARD7 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: we have identified the molecular basis of FAME2 is an inserted expanded ATTTC repeat in the first intron of the STARD7 gene

checks.claim: In affected members of FAME2 families, the inserted ATTTC repeat expansion in STARD7 intron 1 was accompanied by an expanded endogenous ATTTT repeat.
checks.evidence_quote: The pathogenic ATTTC insertion and expansion was always accompanied by the endogenous ATTTT pentanucleotide repeat in all cases of FAME2 that we describe here
checks.explanation: Supported together with the stated 'expansion of an ATTTT repeat'.

checks.claim: On the forward strand of chromosome 2, the FAME2-associated STARD7 repeat had the structure (AAATG)n(AAAAT)n.
checks.evidence_quote: This suggested the structure of the pathogenic repeat in the context of the forward strand of chr2 was (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n
checks.explanation: The paper includes an unknown [N] spacer between the two repeat blocks, which the draft omits.

checks.claim: The FAME2-associated STARD7 repeat expansion was found by whole-genome sequencing and repeat-primed PCR.
checks.evidence_quote: Using whole genome sequencing and repeat primed PCR, we provide evidence that chr2-linked FAME (FAME2) is caused by an expansion of an ATTTC pentamer

checks.claim: The STARD7 repeat expansion segregated in 158 of 158 typically affected individuals in FAME2 families.
checks.evidence_quote: The ATTTC expansions segregate in 158/158 individuals typically affected by FAME from 22 pedigrees

checks.claim: The STARD7 repeat expansion was absent from 69 control genomes.
checks.evidence_quote: The ATTTC repeat was not present in any whole-genome sequencing data from 69 control samples

checks.claim: The STARD7 repeat expansion was absent from 28 control DNA samples.
checks.evidence_quote: The ATTTC repeat expansion did not amplify in any of 28 control DNA samples extracted from unaffected individuals unrelated to FAME.

checks.claim: Long-read sequencing of one FAME2 patient showed 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats in a SMRT read of the STARD7 expansion.
checks.evidence_quote: The SMRT read generated to 99% base accuracy by circular consensus calling was comprised of four subreads and contained 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats

checks.claim: Long-read sequencing of the same FAME2 patient showed 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats in a nanopore read of the STARD7 expansion.
checks.evidence_quote: The Oxford Nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats with some interruptions

checks.claim: The differing repeat counts between SMRT and nanopore reads in one FAME2 patient suggested somatic instability of the STARD7 repeat expansion.
checks.evidence_quote: suggesting somatic variation of repeat sizes may occur within the one individual
checks.explanation: Stated; the paper also says the expansions 'may be somatically unstable'.

checks.claim: Another FAME2 patient had a STARD7 expansion of 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats, totaling 4,645 bp.
checks.evidence_quote: a single Oxford Nanopore read spanned the expanded repeats with 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats; 4645 bp in total length

checks.claim: STARD7 mRNA levels were not altered in fibroblasts from FAME2 patients.
checks.evidence_quote: showed no significant differences in STARD7 transcript expression in patient-derived fibroblast cell lines

checks.claim: STARD7 protein levels were not altered in fibroblasts from FAME2 patients.
checks.evidence_quote: Protein abundance was also unaltered, confirmed by western blotting

agent.process_note: I read all 10 files. Two were full texts and were read in full: De Fusco 2014 on ADRA2B and Corbett 2019 on STARD7. Seven were available only as abstracts, and Saint-Martin 2008 only as a title, which I cited only for what its title states. I searched for zygosity terms and found no paper that explicitly calls the STARD7 expansion heterozygous. For that reason the intro states no zygosity, and inheritance is given as autosomal dominant, on the evidence of the linkage and segregation reports. No gene MIM number or cytogenetic band was supplied, so none was written. I left Labauge 2002 uncited because its abstract only excludes 8q24 in a European FAME family and does not link that family to chromosome 2. The STARD7 expansion has no HGVS name in the paper, so its hgvs list is empty. The ADRA2B indel is listed as a variant of unknown significance because Corbett 2019 found the STARD7 expansion in both families that carry it.
